title: Day 3 Knowledge Check: Externalized Prompts & Local SLM Inference

questions.question: Why store prompts in external YAML files (configs/prompts/*.yaml) instead of Python f-strings?

options.A: To enable versioned prompt updates, hot-reloading, and clean separation between code and prompt tuning.
options.B: Because Python strings cannot hold more than 256 characters.
options.C: Because YAML automatically fine-tunes Qwen weights.

questions.explanation: Externalized YAML prompts let teams iterate on instructions and hyperparameters without redeploying Python logic.
questions.implication: Prompt changes can be reviewed in Git PRs, rolled back independently, and hot-reloaded without container rebuilds.

questions.question: How should you structure prompts to maximize KV / Prompt Caching savings on OpenAI, Gemini, or local vLLM?

options.A: Put the dynamic raw_log at the very top and system instructions at the bottom.
options.B: Place static system instructions and shared runbooks first, and dynamic incident logs at the end.
options.C: Randomize the system prompt on every request.

questions.explanation: Prefix KV caching reuses attention tensors only for identical leading token prefixes.
questions.implication: Putting dynamic timestamps or log lines at token 0 invalidates prefix caching on every call, inflating latency and cloud token bills by 50–80%.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of running a 1.5B Small Language Model (SLM) locally during workshops and edge triage?

options.A: Zero marginal token cost, full offline determinism, and zero data egress.
options.B: It has more parameters than frontier cloud models.
options.C: It requires no RAM or CPU.

questions.explanation: Local SLMs eliminate API rate limits, network flakiness, and PII egress risks.
questions.implication: Sensitive production logs containing internal hostnames or customer IDs never leave your VPC or workstation.
